author: myra-houser
description: In 1948, Stalin cut the railways and waterways leading to West Berlin: the city faced starvation. For fifteen months, the Western powers would feed it from the sky.

hero.hook: When Stalin closed the roads to West Berlin, only one way in remained: the sky.

blocks.text: In **1948**, the Berlin [[airlift]] became the first visible symbol of the [[Cold War]], the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union that would divide the world. It answered the [[Berlin Blockade]] imposed by the Soviets and turned into a humanitarian mission lasting more than a year. It was both the consequence and the accelerator of the split between East Berlin and West Berlin.

Some images endure: planes landing without pause, children perched on the rubble to watch them, a pilot dropping candy by parachute. Carried by the press, they won America future allies and would outlive the whole Cold War. Why did a capital city have to be fed from the sky?

World War II ended in **1945**. The victorious [[Allies]] chose to rebuild the former Axis countries, Germany and Japan. The lesson came from the previous war: Germany's economic ruin after 1918 had opened the way to extremism and to the Nazi party. To prevent a third world war, the country was divided into zones, each entrusted to one of the victors.

blocks.caption: Occupied Germany (1945-1949): four zones, and Berlin itself divided in the heart of the Soviet zone.

blocks.text: France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States each received a zone. Berlin, the capital, lay deep inside the Soviet zone, but the city was itself split into **four** sectors. Bonn would serve as the capital of West Germany; Berlin nonetheless remained an essential city.

Yet the victors over Nazism had almost nothing in common. Since the Russian Revolution of **1917**, Russia, now the Soviet Union, had lived under a communist system, a model the United States rejected. During the war, the two countries had already raced each other to develop the nuclear bomb.

Two superpowers now faced each other in a contest for global influence. France and the United Kingdom sided with the United States. Germany was cut in two: the West, tied to the Americans and their allies, and the East, tied to the Soviets. Each ran its zone according to its own model. Berliners, for their part, ended up in whichever sector they had been assigned.
The dividing line respected nothing: it often ran straight through families and cut in two neighborhoods that had always lived together.

sections.title: From allies to enemies: the East-West split

blocks.text: In early **1948**, the Allied powers met to discuss Germany's future and to consider handing it back to the Germans. [[Stalin]], the master of the Soviet Union, announced that he would ignore their conclusions. He then ordered what became known as the Berlin Blockade, to force the Western powers out of the city. Rail and water routes were cut. West Berlin, which depended on deliveries from the Allied zones, could no longer feed itself.

blocks.caption: American pilot Gail Halvorsen, the "Candy Bomber," ties sweets to small handkerchief parachutes (1948).

blocks.text: The United States, France and the United Kingdom, joined by Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa, then supplied the city by air. The Americans called their share of the effort **Operation Vittles**; the whole undertaking went down in history as the Berlin Airlift, and it lasted **fifteen months**. One pilot, nicknamed the [[Candy Bomber]], dropped candy tied to makeshift parachutes for the children: his images earned America a great deal of goodwill.

Faced with East Berlin's economic troubles, Stalin finally reopened the transit routes. The Allies still kept up a few supply flights. The blockade had failed: the Western powers stayed in Berlin, and the divided city now embodied the East-West confrontation.

The blockade and the airlift made Berlin the first concrete symbol of the Cold War. Tensions did not ease. In **1961**, the East German government built the [[Berlin Wall]] to stop its people from fleeing to the West. In **1963**, US President John F. Kennedy came to the city and declared "Ich bin ein Berliner," "I am a Berliner," as a sign of solidarity with the city.

blocks.caption: The Wall seen from West Berlin in 1989: the death strip and an East German watchtower in front of the buildings of East Berlin.

blocks.text: The Wall stood for **28 years**. On **9 November 1989**, as the Cold War faded, it finally opened. Berliners climbed onto it with hammers and chisels to tear it down themselves. These images, and those of families reunited after years of separation, went around the world. For many, the fall of the Wall marked the end of the Cold War, just as the airlift had marked its beginning.

events.title: Fall of the Wall

blocks.text: In 1948, the Soviet blockade set out to drive the Western powers from Berlin; the fifteen-month airlift fed the city, defeated Stalin and made Berlin the symbol of the Cold War, from its beginning to its end.
